s: Part six.
Review architectures.
By the end of this part, you'll know the four ways to spend extra effort on review, what each one catches and misses, and the one blind spot they all share.
Let's start with a picture.
People are bad at proofreading their own writing.
Why?
Because they read what they meant to write.
A colleague who never saw your draft catches the missing word on the first pass.
This part is about spending extra effort on review wisely.
There are several ways to check work.
One.
A fresh reviewer.
Two.
A second pass that checks each claim against the source.
Three.
Several reviewers, working independently.
Four.
A cheap first pass that escalates only the hard cases.
Each one catches different errors, costs different amounts, and has a blind spot.
The exam wants you to match the architecture to the failure, and to the budget.
Start with self-review.
In exam terms, an instance reviewing its own output keeps its conversation history.
And it keeps the reasoning it used to justify its choices.
So it's unlikely to question them.
That's called self-review bias.
The fix is an independent instance, with fresh context.
It sees only the output, such as a diff plus the review criteria.
Not the writer's history.
The course signal is explicit.
Hold on to this line.
Better review means independent instances, not prompting the same instance to be more careful.
Next, the two architectures the notes distinguish.
The first is multi-pass.
Multi-pass is sequential.
Each pass sees the previous pass's output.
Pass one extracts.
Pass two verifies each extracted value against the source.
It quotes the supporting text.
And it sets anything it can't support to null.
Pass three adjudicates.
What is it strong on?
Errors of commission.
That means fabricated or unsupported values.
Why?
Because the verification pass isn't invested in the first answer.
It costs roughly two to three times a single pass.
And for code review, the multi-pass idea takes a specific shape.
Parallel per-file passes, for depth.
Then an integration pass over their findings, for cross-file breadth.
The second is multi-instance.
Multi-instance is parallel and independent.
You run the same input through several separate calls that can't see each other.
And you compare.
It costs roughly N times, plus adjudication.
Now here's the key.
The valuable output isn't the majority answer.
It's which fields disagreed.
Disagreement localises genuine ambiguity.
And it tells you exactly what to send to a person.
So the rule is this.
Hold on to this line.
Use disagreement to route, not to vote.
And here's the blind spot both share.
Picture three judges, all handed a rulebook with the same mistake in it.
They all make the same wrong call.
And they agree perfectly.
Does adding a fourth judge with the same rulebook help?
No.
You have to fix the rulebook.
In exam terms: unanimity is not correctness.
Every instance reads the same criterion.
So a flawed criterion produces confident, agreeing, wrong answers.
And the high agreement reads as high confidence.
Which is worse than no signal.
No review architecture fixes a bad criterion.
The fix goes back to part one.
Finally, tiered escalation.
This is the answer the exam usually wants when volume and budget appear in the same stem.
Picture airport security.
They don't hand-search every bag.
And they don't pick bags at random.
They search the ones the scanner flags, or that look unusual.
And every so often, they check a few unflagged bags, to make sure the scanner isn't missing something.
In exam terms: run one cheap, schema-enforced pass over everything.
Then escalate only the flagged subset to verification, or to multi-instance review.
That lands near one point two to one point five times the single-pass cost.
Compare that with three times for uniform review.
So what should trigger escalation?
Signals that need no second model call.
There are three kinds.
One.
Tier two and tier three validation failures, from part four.
Two.
A confidence field whose values are tied to observable document properties.
Such as "low if handwritten, rotated, partially illegible, or an unrecognised layout."
Three.
Properties known before the call.
Such as page count, scan quality, and whether you recognise the layout.
And there's a remaining risk.
The trigger might miss some hard documents.
The technical term is triage recall.
So you periodically sample the unescalated population, to check.
Why not just ask the model for a confidence score?
A free-floating, self-reported score is a model output like any other.
It's under the same pressure to fabricate as the data.
And it tends to read high on exactly the well-formatted wrong answers you most want to catch.
Tying the enum to observable properties turns a feeling into a checkable condition.
Quick recap before the questions.
Fresh eyes beat self-review.
Multi-pass catches made-up values.
Multi-instance finds genuine disagreement, and you route on it.
Tiered escalation spends extra only on the hard cases.
And none of them fixes a bad rulebook.
Right.
Four practice questions.
Question one.
Here's the scenario.
A developer uses Claude Code to implement a payment-retry feature.
Then, in the same session, asks it to review its changes carefully.
It approves.
And a race condition surfaces in staging.
What's the fix?
Take a second.
The answer.
Have a separate instance review the diff.
One with no access to the writing session's history.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: ask the same session to review "as a skeptical senior engineer."
Why?
That changes the persona.
But it leaves the same history and justifications.
Wrong: add "double-check every line thoroughly."
Why?
It adds no new perspective.
Wrong: raise the writing session's reasoning effort.
Why?
It still starts from its own justifications.
And that's the source of the blind spot.
We saw the same isolation idea in the chapter on agent architecture, where subagents get fresh context by design.
Question two.
Here's the scenario.
A single review instance reads entire twenty-five-file pull requests, in one pass.
Feedback is shallow.
And it misses bugs where a changed function signature in one file breaks callers in another.
Reviews are pre-merge, and must finish in minutes.
What's the fix?
Take a second.
The answer.
Per-file review passes, in parallel.
Then an integration pass over their findings, for cross-file issues.
Here's the picture.
One inspector walking a whole house in ten minutes notices the paint.
Now send one inspector to each room at once.
Then have a lead walk the house, checking how the rooms connect.
And you find the pipe running from the bathroom into the kitchen ceiling.
Running the per-file passes in parallel is what keeps it inside the time budget.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: "be thorough and check cross-file impact."
Why?
It doesn't change what one overloaded pass can attend to.
And the course verdict on this exact move is no.
Wrong: five instances over the whole pull request, with majority voting.
Why?
It costs five times as much.
It keeps the same shallow approach.
And it throws away the disagreements that would locate real issues.
Wrong: batch.
Why?
Batch can't sit behind a merge gate.
And it doesn't make a review deeper.
That ties back to part five.
Question three.
Here's the scenario.
A claims-document pipeline processes three hundred thousand documents a month, with one enforced-schema pass.
About five percent are hard.
Scans, handwriting, unusual layouts.
Leadership will fund at most about one point five times current cost.
What should trigger verification?
Take a second.
The answer.
Validation failures.
A confidence enum tied to handwriting or rotation.
And scan quality.
Plus audits of the unescalated documents.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: a self-reported score from zero to one hundred, with escalation below eighty.
Why?
A free-floating score is under fabrication pressure.
Wrong: a random five percent daily sample, chosen to match the known rate of hard documents.
That sounds clever.
Why is it wrong?
Matching the rate is not matching the documents.
Random sampling doesn't correlate with difficulty.
So it verifies mostly clean files, and lets most hard ones through.
Wrong: three independent instances on every document.
Why?
That costs about three times.
Well over the ceiling.
Question four.
Here's the scenario.
A research system classifies sources as primary or secondary.
It runs three independent instances, and sends only disagreements to a human.
An audit finds many unanimous "primary" verdicts are wrong.
News articles re-reporting a company press release are consistently labelled primary.
What's the fix?
Take a second.
The answer.
Rewrite the primary-source criterion.
With explicit tests.
An exclusion for re-reported press material.
And near-miss examples.
For instance.
Primary only if the author or publisher is the originating party, and the content isn't a restatement of another document.
And: do not classify news re-reporting a press release as primary.
Then show the press release itself as primary.
And an article quoting it as secondary.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: five instances instead of three.
Why?
They just agree more loudly.
Wrong: a verification pass re-applying the same definition to every unanimous verdict.
That sounds like multi-pass rigour.
Why is it wrong?
It confirms the same wrong labels.
Multi-pass misses systematic misreadings that every pass shares.
Wrong: lower temperature.
Why?
It increases agreement on the wrong answer.
And it strengthens the misleading signal.
Let me pull the architectures into one spoken comparison.
Four of them.
One.
A single pass, with explicit criteria and an enforced schema.
It costs one times.
It catches format errors, and what the criteria cover.
It fits when errors are cheap, or a human reads everything anyway.
Two.
Multi-pass verification.
It costs two to three times.
It catches fabricated values and unsupported claims.
It misses shared misreadings.
And it fits when fabrication is the main failure, and the source is available to re-check.
The notes give one such case.
Values that appear nowhere in the source.
A budget of about double.
And the document always available.
That points to a second pass that quotes and nulls.
Three.
Multi-instance.
It costs N times, plus adjudication.
It catches genuine ambiguity, and unstable boundary calls.
It misses errors caused by the criteria.
And it fits when judgment is contested, and you need a signal to route on.
Four.
Tiered escalation.
It costs about one point two to one point five times.
It catches most of the above, on the subset that needs it.
It misses whatever the trigger fails to flag.
And it fits high volume with a minority of hard cases.
Which is the usual production reality.
Two contrasts to lock this in.
First.
Multi-pass versus multi-instance.
Multi-pass is sequential, and catches things that were made up.
Multi-instance is parallel, and catches things that are genuinely debatable.
Neither catches a bad rulebook.
Second, a contrast that spans the chapter.
When a review fails, is it the architecture, or the criterion?
If all the reviewers agree and are wrong, it's the criterion.
If a single reviewer is shallow across many files, it's the architecture.
If the reviewer wrote the code, it's self-review bias.
And the words in a question that should switch this part on.
"Same session reviews its own work."
That means independent instance.
"Many files, shallow, cross-file bugs, must finish in minutes."
That means parallel per-file passes, plus integration.
"Volume" and "budget ceiling," together.
That means tiered escalation, with observable triggers.
"Unanimous but wrong."
That means fix the criterion.
"Values not in the source, source available, about double the budget."
That means multi-pass verification, with quotes.
That's part six.
If you remember one thing, make it this.
Use fresh eyes, buy extra review only where the hard cases are, route on disagreement rather than voting, and remember no amount of review fixes a bad rulebook.
Coming up next: the trap round.
The trap round.
Here comes the rapid-fire round.
Each one is a pattern you might see in an answer option, and the thought it should trigger.
We'll go part by part.
First, criteria.
If you see "be more careful," "be conservative," or "be thorough," think: no boundary.
Write named tests and an exclusion list.
If you see capital letters, "serious error," or "will be audited," think: emphasis is persuasion.
And it can cause overtriggering.
If you see "only keep findings above zero point nine confidence," think: self-reported confidence is not calibrated to your standards.
And a global threshold mutes the good categories too.
If you see "set temperature to zero," think: determinism is not precision.
Same answer, just as wrong.
If you see "run it three times and keep what they all agree on," think: they share the same criterion.
So they agree on the same mistake.
If you see one category above about sixty percent false positives, while the rest are fine, think: disable that category alone, with a re-enable date.
If you see "uncertain cases must stay visible," think: a required needs_human_review outcome.
Next, examples.
If you see one example per label, or examples from the highest-volume cases, think: no boundary information.
Spend them on the disputed cases.
If you see every example showing the same outcome, think: that teaches a lean.
Balance the outcomes.
If you see examples with only inputs and outputs, failing on a new layout, think: show the reasoning.
Next, structured output.
If you see "JSON only" in the prompt, with a growing repair layer, think: a forced tool call, or Structured Outputs.
If you see "prefill an opening brace," think: retired on Claude four point six and later.
And incompatible with enforcement.
If you see tool_choice auto for mandatory extraction, think: the model can skip the tool.
Force it.
If you see a required field that can't be null, and invented values, think: string or null, still required, plus fields_not_found.
If you see "remove it from required," think: you lose the presence guarantee.
If you see "add a pattern," or "add a maximum length," to stop wrong values, think: patterns check shape.
Length bounds are not enforced.
And invented values are well formed.
Use an enum if the values can be listed.
If you see --output-format json at the command line, and a free-text answer, think: that's the envelope.
Use --json-schema, and read structured_output.
Next, validation and retries.
If you see "Validation failed, please try again," think: name the field, the value, the rule and the next step.
As a tool result with is_error true.
If you see "raise the retry cap," "add backoff," or "use a bigger model," think: none of these add information.
Fix the feedback.
If you see the pass rate rise, but auditors find changed totals, think: the feedback didn't say which side is authoritative.
If you see a field the document never states, failing every retry, think: stop retrying.
Allow null.
Route to a person.
If you see self-consistent records from the wrong document, think: tier three.
Check against your own reference data.
Next, batch.
If you see "most batches finish within an hour," against a deadline, think: design to the twenty-four-hour worst case.
If you see batch proposed for an agent that reads, then decides what to read next, think: batch is single-turn only.
If you see missing records after a batch ended, with no errors, think: ended is not success.
Switch on all four result types.
If you see results matched by position, think: join on custom_id.
If you see "split into many small batches," think: failure is already per request.
You only add tracking work.
If you see "batch lowers quality," think: same model, same quality.
The issue is only timing.
And last, review architectures.
If you see a session reviewing its own code, think: an independent instance, with fresh context.
If you see a random sample as an escalation trigger, think: random doesn't track difficulty.
If you see uniform three-pass review over a mostly clean corpus, think: tiered escalation, at about one point two to one point five times.
If you see unanimous but wrong, think: fix the criterion, not the topology.
That's the trap round.
Coming up next: the closing recap.
The closing recap.
Here are the ten things to remember from this chapter.
Each one in plain words first, then its technical name.
One.
A model that flags everything isn't confused.
It's guessing where your line is.
So draw the line.
The technical name is explicit categorical or conjunctive criteria, with an exclusion list.
Two.
Give the model a truthful way to say "I am not sure," and a place to say it.
That's an abstention channel.
Usually a required needs_human_review outcome.
Plus stating that an empty result is valid.
Three.
Confidence scores and lower randomness feel like fixes.
But they don't move the line.
The technical terms are self-reported confidence, which is not calibrated to your standards.
And temperature, where determinism is not precision.
Four.
When one part of a reviewer is noisy, switch off just that part, with a date to bring it back.
That's disabling a single category above roughly sixty percent false positives, with the re-enable date in the prompt.
Five.
Teach with the hard cases, not the easy ones.
And show the reasoning.
That's targeted few-shot prompting at the fault lines.
Boundary cases.
Near misses on both sides.
Balanced outcomes.
Matched surface features.
Input, then reasoning, then output.
In example tags.
Six.
Stop asking for the right format, and make any other format impossible.
That's a forced tool call using tool_choice.
Or Structured Outputs, using output_config.format.
With enum for listable values.
And at the command line, the --json-schema flag, with the answer in structured_output.
Seven.
A form with no box for "not stated" collects guesses.
That's typing optional fields as string or null, keeping them required, and adding a fields_not_found list.
Eight.
A neat answer can still be false.
So check it against itself, and against the world.
Those are tier two internal and tier three external validation.
Because a schema guarantees shape, never truth.
Nine.
When you send work back, say exactly what's wrong, and which figure to trust.
And stop after a couple of tries, or when the information simply isn't there.
That's a tool result with is_error true, naming field, value, rule and next action.
A bounded retry cap of two or three, depending on the source.
And routing absent data to a person.
Ten.
Use the cheap overnight service only when nobody is waiting, and each job is one round trip.
And spend extra review only where the hard cases are.
That's the Message Batches API at half price, with custom_id joins, and all four result types handled.
And tiered escalation with independent reviewers, where unanimity is never mistaken for correctness.
That's Domain four.
Six task statements, ten things to remember, and twenty percent of the exam.
If you remember one sentence, make it this one.
Hold on to this line.
A schema guarantees shape, never truth.
And every other technique in this chapter exists to close that gap.
